description:
We are two 3rd-year Business Technology undergraduates from the University of Kelaniya who are passionate about building apps. 

For the Space Mission Design Game challenge, we are creating an interactive experience where players design spacecraft, select scientific instruments, choose launch vehicles and orbits, and manage real engineering trade-offs such as budget, mass, power, communications, and mission lifetime. Our goal is to make complex space mission concepts accessible and educational.
summary:
Mission Architect: Red Frontier is a free, mobile-friendly space adventure game that teaches students the engineering decisions behind a complete science mission. Players harvest fictional resources, run a supply shop, hire workers and automate production, then spend their earnings on scientific exploration, either solo or in a shared online colony with up to three friends.

To launch a mission, players choose a scientific objective, spacecraft, instruments, power systems, communications equipment, orbit and launch vehicle. Each choice affects mass, energy, data return, cost and scientific capability. Mission reviews explain design problems, and a final science report helps players learn from the consequences and improve their next mission.

This addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by making mission design the core of play, informed by NASA’s mission lifecycle, JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels and CubeSat 101. It matters because it makes real engineering trade-offs accessible and fun for learners. Built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript, Canvas 2D and WebSockets, with AI assistance clearly disclosed.
details:
Mission Architect: Red Frontier is a free, mobile-friendly space adventure that helps students experience the engineering decisions behind a complete science mission. Players can explore alone or cooperate with up to three friends in a shared online colony.

Players harvest fictional resources, process supplies, operate a supply shop, and hire workers to automate production. Their earnings fund scientific exploration. Equipment upgrades, exploration challenges, special orders and new colony sectors provide progression while keeping mission design central to the game.

To launch a mission, players choose a scientific objective, spacecraft, instruments, power systems, communications equipment, orbit and launch vehicle. These choices affect mass, energy, data return, cost and scientific capability. Mission reviews explain design problems, while an operating decision and final science report help players understand the consequences and improve their next mission.

NASA’s Design and Develop Science Missions informed the mission lifecycle, requirements and launch, space, ground and user segments. JPL’s Concept Maturity Levels informed staged review and iteration. CubeSat 101 supported spacecraft-development and ground-communications learning content. Numerical values are simplified educational models; the game does not use live NASA telemetry.

The project uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, TypeScript, Canvas 2D and WebSockets, with Higgsfield providing the build environment and hosting. Its creative approach connects an accessible idle adventure to meaningful engineering trade-offs. Touch controls, cooperative play, saved progress and bounded idle production support different playing styles. Testing included 75 automated checks and live two-player verification of production, missions, reconnects and idle accounting.

AI-use disclosure: The team supplied the project direction and gameplay preferences. OpenAI Codex assisted with research, design development, code, explanatory text, tests and verification. GPT Image 2.6 through Higgsfield generated the original cartoon artwork. Generated artwork is visibly labelled, and source metadata records AI assistance. The demonstration is recorded gameplay containing AI-generated artwork. Original code and asset credits are publicly available.
